title: One rule for what starts the motion loop playing
goal: Three things you can do to a motion answer the question does this start it playing in three different ways. Adding a motion starts the loop on its own. Grabbing the pivot on the picture starts it if it was stopped. Changing a number on a motion row while it is paused does not start it, so the edit lands and nothing on screen moves and you cannot tell whether it took. Settle one rule for when the app plays without being asked, and make all three follow it.
notes:
Found in the design review of 2026-09-15. Three audits from the same day, each stating its own behaviour and none able to cite the other two:

queue/audits/2026-09-15-layer-motion.json, rough item four: "Editing a field while the preview is PAUSED does not start it: you press play. Adding a motion does start it. Those are two different rules and somebody may well expect one."

queue/audits/2026-09-15-layer-motion.json, evaluate item one: "Adding a motion starts it playing on its own. Is that the right amount of eager, or do you want to press play yourself?"

queue/audits/2026-09-15-motion-pivot.json, evaluate item three: "Grabbing the pivot starts the loop if it is stopped, because a still picture cannot show you a pivot. Is that helpful or is it the app taking over?"

Each of the three was argued honestly on its own and each is defensible alone. Together they are three answers to one question, shipped within eight hours of each other, and the person meeting them is meeting all three in one sitting. The pivot case has the strongest argument for starting the loop (a still picture cannot show you a pivot), so it is the one to reason from rather than the one to change first.

Not seen on a screen: the Mac has been locked since 2026-09-14 20:46:47, so none of the three was ever run in a walk. The behaviours are read from the audits the runners wrote from their own code, not from watching the app.
acceptance: There is one written rule for when the motion loop starts without being asked, and it is in the audit or the design doc rather than only in the code
Adding a motion, grabbing the pivot, and editing a number on a paused motion all follow that one rule
Editing a number while paused never leaves a change that landed with nothing on screen to show it, whatever the rule turns out to be
A walk drives all three in one run and reads back whether the loop is playing after each

log.note: Another place the rule now has to cover: a tutorial sample that arrives already moving. Three of the new Icons guides (get-the-timing-right, two-parts-out-of-phase, export-an-animated-svg) open on a bell that swings and say so on their first card, and until 2026-09-15 that card was a lie, because opening a document with motion in it did not start the loop. EditorState.openTutorialSample now calls playMotionPreview() when the sample has motion, deliberately scoped to a guide's own sample rather than to opening any document. Whatever one rule is settled on, that special case should fold into it rather than stay beside it.

Adversarial review BEFORE building. Three candidate rules. (a) 'the app never starts the loop, only the play button does' is what the mock did and the design doc already rejected it: add a motion and nothing whatsoever happens, which is a feature that looks broken on the first press. (b) 'an edit while paused plays one lap and then goes back to paused' honours the pause and is nicer for a typed number, but it breaks on the two DRAGS: let go of the pivot and the loop would stop, which snaps the shape back to nought degrees on every release, a jump cut in the middle of the gesture. It also needs a second kind of playing that the play button has to somehow express. (c) 'motion plays unless you stop it' is one sentence, no modes, and its only cost - a pause lost when you change a number - is repaired by one click on a button that is on screen in three places. What rescues (c) is that changing the DRAWING is not changing the motion, so pausing to work on the picture still keeps the picture still, which is the workflow pause actually exists for. Built (c), the shortest version that delivers the value.

Review AFTER building, done by reading rather than by using it: the Mac's screen has been locked since 2026-09-14 20:46, so no walk can run and no picture of the app is possible. Two things the read turned up. First, a real defect the rule surfaced: canPlayMotion asked whether a LAP LENGTH existed rather than whether anything was switched on, and a lap dragged onto the strip stays written down after every row on it is switched off, so the play button stayed live over a picture where nothing moved - and under the new rule the next number typed would have started a loop of a still icon. It now asks automaticMotionCycleLengthMS > 0, which is the question about what is ON. Second, left rough rather than filed: dragging inside the colour well on a Color motion writes a value continuously and each write now starts the lap over, so the preview sits pinned at the top of the lap while your hand is in the colour wheel. It did the same before this change whenever the preview was already running, so it is not new, it is only reachable from stopped now too; a person would barely notice and nothing is broken, so it stays here rather than becoming a near-twin task. Also left rough: undo and redo deliberately do NOT start the loop, on the grounds that they put back a picture you have already seen. That is the one place the rule could reasonably have gone the other way, and it is in the audit's rough list for the user to disagree with.
